notes:
1. Basic Facts
  • Light is a form of electromagnetic radiation.
  • Light enables vision by carrying information from objects to the eye.
  • Light can travel through vacuum.
  • Light does not require a material medium.
  • The speed of light in vacuum is approximately 3 × 10⁸ m/s.
  • Light travels more slowly in transparent material media than in vacuum.
  • Visible light is only a small part of the electromagnetic spectrum.
  • Light shows reflection, refraction, interference, diffraction and polarisation.
  • Light exhibits wave-particle duality.
  • Light energy is carried in discrete packets called photons.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Light → Electromagnetic Wave → No Medium Required

2. Speed of Light
  • Speed of light in vacuum is represented by c.
  • c ≈ 3 × 10⁸ m/s.
  • Light travels fastest in vacuum.
  • In a transparent medium, speed v = c/n.
  • n is the refractive index of the medium.
  • Greater refractive index generally means lower light speed in that medium.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

c ≈ 3 × 10⁸ m/s

3. Photon
  • A photon is a quantum of electromagnetic radiation.
  • Photon energy is E = hf.
  • h is Planck's constant.
  • f is frequency.
  • Photon energy is also E = hc/λ.
  • Higher frequency means greater photon energy.
  • Shorter wavelength means greater photon energy.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Photon Energy → E = hf = hc/λ

4. Visible Light
  • Visible light is the part of the electromagnetic spectrum detectable by the human eye.
  • Visible wavelengths are approximately 400 nm to 700 nm.
  • Violet has shorter wavelength than red.
  • Red has longer wavelength than violet.
  • Violet light has higher frequency than red light.
  • Violet photons have greater energy than red photons.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Red → Long wavelength, low frequency

Violet → Short wavelength, high frequency

5. Rectilinear Propagation of Light
  • Light travels approximately in straight lines in a uniform transparent medium.
  • This property is called rectilinear propagation of light.
  • Formation of shadows is evidence for rectilinear propagation.
  • Pinhole cameras operate using rectilinear propagation.
  • Eclipses can be explained geometrically using straight-line propagation of light.
6. Shadow
  • A shadow forms when an opaque object blocks light.
  • Umbra is the region of complete shadow.
  • Penumbra is the region of partial shadow.
  • A point source can produce a sharp shadow.
  • An extended light source can produce both umbra and penumbra.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Umbra → Complete shadow

Penumbra → Partial shadow

7. Transparent Material
  • Transparent materials allow most visible light to pass through.
  • Clear glass is transparent.
  • Pure water is transparent.
  • Transparent materials allow objects behind them to be seen clearly.
8. Translucent Material
  • Translucent materials allow some light to pass but scatter it strongly.
  • Objects cannot be seen clearly through translucent materials.
  • Frosted glass is translucent.
  • Butter paper is translucent.
9. Opaque Material
  • Opaque materials do not transmit visible light significantly.
  • Wood is generally opaque.
  • Metals are opaque to visible light in ordinary bulk form.
  • Opaque objects form shadows.
10. Reflection of Light
  • Reflection is the return of light into the same medium after striking a surface.
  • Mirrors produce regular reflection.
  • Rough surfaces produce diffuse reflection.
  • Reflection obeys two fundamental laws.
11. First Law of Reflection
  • Angle of incidence equals angle of reflection.
  • i = r.
  • Both angles are measured from the normal.
  • The law applies to specular reflection.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Reflection → i = r

12. Second Law of Reflection
  • Incident ray, reflected ray and normal lie in the same plane.
  • The normal is drawn perpendicular to the reflecting surface at the point of incidence.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Angles are measured from the normal, not from the mirror surface.

13. Regular Reflection
  • Regular reflection occurs from smooth surfaces.
  • Parallel incident rays remain orderly after reflection.
  • A clear image can be formed.
  • Plane mirrors exhibit regular reflection.
14. Diffuse Reflection
  • Diffuse reflection occurs from rough surfaces.
  • Reflected rays scatter in many directions.
  • Each ray still obeys the laws of reflection locally.
  • Diffuse reflection allows ordinary objects to be seen from many directions.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Diffuse reflection does not violate the laws of reflection.

15. Plane Mirror
  • A plane mirror has a flat reflecting surface.
  • It forms a virtual image.
  • Image is erect.
  • Image is the same size as the object.
  • Image distance behind mirror equals object distance in front.
  • Image shows lateral inversion.
  • Plane mirror image cannot be obtained on a screen.
📌 Must-Memorise

Plane Mirror → Virtual + Erect + Same Size + Laterally Inverted

16. Lateral Inversion
  • Lateral inversion is apparent left-right reversal in a plane mirror.
  • Top and bottom are not interchanged.
  • The phenomenon is important in mirror writing.
  • The word AMBULANCE is often written in reverse on the front of vehicles so drivers can read it correctly in rear-view mirrors.
17. Number of Images Between Two Mirrors
  • Two parallel plane mirrors can produce many repeated images.
  • When mirrors are inclined, the number depends on the angle between them.
  • A common relation is approximately N = 360°/θ − 1 when 360°/θ is an integer under standard arrangement.
  • If the ratio is not an integer, the exact number depends on geometry and object position.
18. Spherical Mirrors
  • Spherical mirrors are parts of spherical reflecting surfaces.
  • They are of two types: concave and convex.
  • A concave mirror has reflecting surface curved inward.
  • A convex mirror has reflecting surface bulging outward.
19. Terms Used in Spherical Mirrors
  • Pole is the geometric centre of the mirror surface.
  • Centre of curvature is centre of the sphere of which the mirror forms a part.
  • Radius of curvature is distance between pole and centre of curvature.
  • Principal axis passes through pole and centre of curvature.
  • Principal focus is the point where parallel rays converge or appear to diverge after reflection.
  • Focal length is distance between pole and focus.
20. Radius of Curvature and Focal Length

For a spherical mirror:

  • f = R/2.
  • R = 2f.
  • This relation is valid for paraxial rays in spherical mirrors.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Mirror → R = 2f

21. Concave Mirror
  • Concave mirror is a converging mirror.
  • Parallel rays reflected from a concave mirror converge at the principal focus.
  • Its principal focus is real.
  • It can form real or virtual images depending on object position.
  • It is used when magnification or concentration of light is required.
22. Convex Mirror
  • Convex mirror is a diverging mirror.
  • Reflected rays diverge.
  • They appear to originate from a virtual focus behind the mirror.
  • A convex mirror always forms a virtual, erect and diminished image for a real object.
  • It gives a wide field of view.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Convex Mirror → Virtual + Erect + Diminished + Wide Field

23. Uses of Convex Mirror
  • Rear-view mirrors in vehicles.
  • Side-view mirrors.
  • Security mirrors in shops.
  • Mirrors at blind road corners.
  • Their wide field of view allows larger areas to be observed.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Vehicle Rear-View Mirror → Convex Mirror

24. Uses of Concave Mirror
  • Shaving mirrors.
  • Dentist mirrors.
  • Makeup mirrors.
  • Reflectors in torches and headlights.
  • Solar furnaces.
  • Reflecting telescopes use concave reflecting surfaces.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Shaving/Dentist Mirror → Concave

25. Concave Mirror — Object Beyond C
  • Image forms between C and F.
  • Image is real.
  • Image is inverted.
  • Image is diminished.
26. Concave Mirror — Object at C
  • Image forms at C.
  • Image is real.
  • Image is inverted.
  • Image is same size as object.
27. Concave Mirror — Object Between C and F
  • Image forms beyond C.
  • Image is real.
  • Image is inverted.
  • Image is enlarged.
28. Concave Mirror — Object at F
  • Reflected rays become parallel.
  • Image is considered at infinity.
  • Image is highly enlarged in ideal treatment.
29. Concave Mirror — Object Between F and Pole
  • Image forms behind the mirror.
  • Image is virtual.
  • Image is erect.
  • Image is enlarged.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Concave + Object within focal length → Virtual, erect, magnified

30. Mirror Formula

For spherical mirrors:

  • 1/f = 1/v + 1/u.
  • f is focal length.
  • v is image distance.
  • u is object distance.
  • Distances are assigned signs according to the chosen sign convention.
31. Magnification in Mirrors
  • Linear magnification m = Image height/Object height.
  • For spherical mirrors, m = −v/u.
  • Positive magnification indicates an erect image in the usual Cartesian convention.
  • Negative magnification indicates an inverted image.
32. Refraction
  • Refraction is the change in direction of light when it passes obliquely from one transparent medium to another.
  • Refraction occurs because light speed changes between media.
  • Light frequency remains unchanged when crossing a stationary boundary.
  • Wavelength changes when light speed changes.
  • Refraction is governed by Snell's Law.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Refraction → Speed changes → Direction may change

33. First Law of Refraction
  • Incident ray, refracted ray and normal lie in the same plane.
34. Snell's Law
  • For two media, n₁ sin i = n₂ sin r.
  • For light entering a second medium from air approximately, refractive index n = sin i/sin r.
  • Willebrord Snell is associated with the law.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Snell → Refraction

35. Refractive Index
  • Absolute refractive index n = c/v.
  • c is speed of light in vacuum.
  • v is speed of light in the medium.
  • Refractive index has no unit.
  • Refractive index is generally greater than or equal to 1 for ordinary transparent materials.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

n = c/v

36. Optically Denser Medium
  • An optically denser medium has a higher refractive index.
  • Light travels more slowly in an optically denser medium.
  • Optical density is not the same as mass density.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Optically denser does not necessarily mean physically denser.

37. Bending Toward Normal
  • Light bends toward the normal when it passes from an optically rarer medium to an optically denser medium.
  • Example: air to glass.
📌 Remember

Rarer → Denser → Toward normal

38. Bending Away from Normal
  • Light bends away from the normal when it passes from an optically denser medium to a rarer medium.
  • Example: glass to air.
📌 Remember

Denser → Rarer → Away from normal

39. Normal Incidence
  • If light strikes the boundary normally, angle of incidence is zero.
  • It passes without deviation in direction.
  • Its speed and wavelength still change between different media.
  • Frequency remains unchanged.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

No bending at normal incidence does not mean speed is unchanged.

40. Apparent Depth
  • An object under water appears shallower when viewed from air.
  • This is caused by refraction.
  • Light bends away from the normal as it passes from water to air.
  • Apparent depth is less than real depth for normal viewing from air.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Object in Water → Appears Raised

41. Refractive Index and Apparent Depth

For near-normal viewing:

  • Refractive index ≈ Real depth / Apparent depth.
  • Apparent depth = Real depth / n.
42. Coin-in-Water Experiment
  • A coin at the bottom of a vessel appears raised after water is added.
  • This demonstrates refraction.
  • The apparent position is closer to the surface than the actual position.
43. Bent Pencil Effect
  • A pencil partly immersed in water appears bent.
  • This is due to refraction at the water-air boundary.
  • Different portions of the pencil are viewed through different optical paths.
44. Glass Slab
  • Light passing obliquely through a rectangular glass slab undergoes refraction twice.
  • Emergent ray is parallel to the incident ray when the slab faces are parallel.
  • The emergent ray is laterally displaced.
  • This displacement is called lateral shift.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Glass Slab → Emergent Ray Parallel + Lateral Shift

45. Total Internal Reflection
  • Total internal reflection is complete reflection of light back into a denser medium.
  • It occurs only when light travels from optically denser to rarer medium.
  • Angle of incidence must exceed the critical angle.
  • At the critical angle, refracted ray travels along the boundary.
  • Above the critical angle, no transmitted refracted ray exists in ideal optics.
📌 Must-Memorise Conditions

Denser → Rarer

i > Critical Angle

46. Critical Angle
  • Critical angle is the angle of incidence in the denser medium for which angle of refraction in the rarer medium is 90°.
  • For a medium relative to air, sin C = 1/n.
  • C is critical angle.
  • Larger refractive index generally gives smaller critical angle.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

sin C = 1/n

47. Applications of Total Internal Reflection
  • Optical fibres.
  • Sparkling of diamonds.
  • Totally reflecting prisms.
  • Some binocular systems.
  • Endoscopes using fibre optics.
  • Telecommunications using optical fibres.
48. Diamond Sparkle
  • Diamond has a high refractive index.
  • Its critical angle is relatively small.
  • Light can undergo repeated total internal reflection.
  • Proper cutting increases internal reflections.
  • Dispersion also contributes to coloured flashes.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Diamond Sparkle → TIR + High Refractive Index

49. Optical Fibre
  • Optical fibre transmits light through a transparent core.
  • Core has higher refractive index than cladding.
  • Light is guided mainly by total internal reflection.
  • Optical fibres carry communication signals.
  • They have high bandwidth.
  • They are immune to ordinary electromagnetic interference.
  • They are also used in medical endoscopy.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Optical Fibre → Total Internal Reflection

50. Core and Cladding
  • Core carries the optical signal.
  • Cladding surrounds the core.
  • Core refractive index is greater than cladding refractive index.
  • This arrangement supports confinement of light within the fibre.
51. Lens
  • A lens is a transparent optical element bounded by two surfaces, at least one usually curved.
  • Lenses refract light.
  • Lenses may be convex or concave.
  • Convex lenses generally converge parallel light.
  • Concave lenses generally diverge parallel light.
52. Convex Lens
  • Convex lens is thicker at the centre than at the edges.
  • It is a converging lens.
  • Parallel rays converge at a real principal focus.
  • It can form real or virtual images.
  • It is used in magnifying glasses and many optical instruments.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Convex Lens → Converging Lens

53. Concave Lens
  • Concave lens is thinner at the centre than at the edges.
  • It is a diverging lens.
  • Parallel rays diverge after passing through it.
  • The rays appear to originate from a virtual focus.
  • For a real object, a concave lens always forms a virtual, erect and diminished image.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Concave Lens → Virtual + Erect + Diminished

54. Important Lens Terms
  • Optical centre is a point near the centre through which a paraxial ray passes with little deviation in a thin lens.
  • Principal axis passes through optical centre.
  • Principal focus is where parallel rays converge or appear to diverge.
  • Focal length is distance between optical centre and focus.
  • Lenses have two principal foci.
55. Convex Lens — Object Beyond 2F
  • Image forms between F and 2F on the other side.
  • Image is real.
  • Image is inverted.
  • Image is diminished.
56. Convex Lens — Object at 2F
  • Image forms at 2F on the other side.
  • Image is real.
  • Image is inverted.
  • Image is same size as object.
57. Convex Lens — Object Between F and 2F
  • Image forms beyond 2F.
  • Image is real.
  • Image is inverted.
  • Image is enlarged.
58. Convex Lens — Object at F
  • Emerging rays become parallel.
  • Image is considered at infinity.
  • Image is highly enlarged in ideal treatment.
59. Convex Lens — Object Between F and Optical Centre
  • Image forms on the same side as object.
  • Image is virtual.
  • Image is erect.
  • Image is enlarged.
  • This is the principle of a simple magnifying glass.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Convex Lens within F → Virtual + Erect + Magnified

60. Lens Formula

For a thin lens:

  • 1/f = 1/v − 1/u using the standard Cartesian sign convention.
  • f is focal length.
  • v is image distance.
  • u is object distance.
61. Lens Magnification
  • Magnification m = Image height/Object height.
  • For a thin lens, m = v/u under the Cartesian sign convention.
  • Positive magnification indicates erect image.
  • Negative magnification indicates inverted image.
62. Power of Lens
  • Power indicates the converging or diverging ability of a lens.
  • P = 1/f when f is measured in metres.
  • SI unit is dioptre.
  • Symbol is D.
  • Convex lens has positive power.
  • Concave lens has negative power.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Lens Power → P = 1/f

63. Dioptre
  • One dioptre is the power of a lens with focal length 1 metre.
  • 1 D = 1 m⁻¹.
  • A lens of focal length 0.5 m has power +2 D if convex.
  • A lens of focal length −0.5 m has power −2 D if concave.
64. Combination of Thin Lenses

For thin lenses in contact:

  • Total power = P₁ + P₂ + P₃ + ...
  • Equivalent focal length follows 1/F = 1/f₁ + 1/f₂ + ...
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Lenses in Contact → Powers Add

65. Prism
  • A prism is a transparent refracting medium bounded by plane surfaces inclined to each other.
  • Light undergoes refraction at both prism surfaces.
  • A prism can deviate light.
  • A prism can disperse white light into colours.
66. Dispersion
  • Dispersion is separation of white light into its component colours.
  • Different wavelengths have different refractive indices in a material.
  • Violet light is usually deviated more than red light in a glass prism.
  • Red light is deviated least among visible colours in ordinary glass.
  • Violet is deviated most.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Prism Dispersion → Violet Most, Red Least

67. VIBGYOR

Visible-spectrum sequence:

  • Violet.
  • Indigo.
  • Blue.
  • Green.
  • Yellow.
  • Orange.
  • Red.
📌 Must-Memorise

VIBGYOR

68. Newton and Dispersion
  • Isaac Newton demonstrated that white light is composed of different colours.
  • He used a prism to produce a spectrum.
  • A second prism can recombine dispersed colours into white light under suitable arrangement.
  • Newton's work showed that the prism separates colours already present in white light.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Newton → Prism → White Light Spectrum

69. Spectrum
  • A spectrum is the distribution of light according to wavelength or frequency.
  • Continuous spectrum contains a continuous range of wavelengths.
  • Emission-line spectra contain bright discrete lines.
  • Absorption spectra contain dark lines or bands where specific wavelengths are absorbed.
  • Spectroscopy is used to identify chemical elements.
70. Spectroscope
  • A spectroscope separates light into its component wavelengths.
  • A prism or diffraction grating may be used.
  • Spectral lines can identify elements.
  • Spectroscopy is important in astronomy and chemistry.
71. Rainbow
  • A rainbow forms through refraction, dispersion and internal reflection of sunlight in water droplets.
  • Primary rainbow has red on the outer edge.
  • Violet appears on the inner edge.
  • A primary rainbow usually involves one internal reflection inside each droplet.
  • A secondary rainbow involves two internal reflections.
  • Colour order is reversed in the secondary rainbow.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Primary Rainbow → Red Outside, Violet Inside

72. Primary Rainbow
  • Formed mainly by refraction, dispersion and one internal reflection.
  • Red appears at the outer side.
  • Violet appears at the inner side.
  • It is brighter than the secondary rainbow.
73. Secondary Rainbow
  • Involves two internal reflections inside raindrops.
  • It appears outside the primary rainbow.
  • It is fainter.
  • Colour sequence is reversed compared with primary rainbow.
74. Scattering of Light
  • Scattering is redirection of light by particles or irregularities.
  • Shorter visible wavelengths are generally scattered more strongly by very small atmospheric particles.
  • Rayleigh scattering intensity varies approximately as 1/λ⁴.
  • This explains several atmospheric colour phenomena.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Rayleigh Scattering → ∝ 1/λ⁴

75. Why the Sky Appears Blue
  • Sunlight contains many visible wavelengths.
  • Small atmospheric molecules scatter shorter wavelengths more strongly.
  • Blue light is strongly scattered toward observers.
  • Violet is scattered even more strongly, but human visual sensitivity and solar spectrum contribute to the sky appearing predominantly blue.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Blue Sky → Rayleigh Scattering

76. Red Colour of Sunrise and Sunset
  • At sunrise and sunset, sunlight travels through a longer atmospheric path.
  • Shorter wavelengths are scattered away more strongly.
  • Longer red and orange wavelengths remain more prominent in direct sunlight.
  • Therefore, Sun and nearby sky appear reddish.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Sunrise/Sunset Red → Longer atmospheric path + scattering

77. Why Danger Signals Are Red
  • Red light has a relatively long wavelength in the visible spectrum.
  • It is scattered less by small particles than shorter wavelengths.
  • Therefore, red can remain visible over relatively long distances under many atmospheric conditions.
  • Red is used for warning and stop signals.
78. Tyndall Effect
  • Tyndall effect is scattering of light by colloidal particles.
  • It makes the path of a light beam visible in a colloid.
  • Dust in a sunbeam can make the beam visible.
  • Fog and smoke can scatter light strongly.
  • True molecular solutions generally do not show a strong Tyndall effect.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Tyndall Effect → Colloidal Scattering

79. Interference
  • Interference occurs when coherent light waves overlap.
  • Constructive interference produces greater intensity.
  • Destructive interference produces reduced intensity.
  • Thomas Young demonstrated light interference using the double-slit experiment.
  • Interference supports the wave nature of light.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Young → Double-Slit → Interference

80. Young's Double-Slit Experiment
  • Two coherent light sources produce alternating bright and dark fringes.
  • Bright fringes correspond mainly to constructive interference.
  • Dark fringes correspond to destructive interference.
  • The experiment provided strong evidence for wave behaviour of light.
81. Diffraction
  • Diffraction is bending and spreading of waves around obstacles or through narrow openings.
  • Diffraction becomes significant when aperture size is comparable to wavelength.
  • Light diffraction supports its wave nature.
  • Diffraction limits the resolving power of optical instruments.
82. Polarisation
  • Polarisation restricts oscillations of a transverse wave to particular directions.
  • Light can be polarised.
  • Polarisation demonstrates the transverse nature of light waves.
  • Polarising filters reduce glare.
  • Sunglasses may use polarising filters.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Polarisation → Light is Transverse

83. Electromagnetic Spectrum

In increasing frequency:

  • Radio waves.
  • Microwaves.
  • Infrared.
  • Visible light.
  • Ultraviolet.
  • X-rays.
  • Gamma rays.
📌 Must-Memorise

Radio → Microwave → IR → Visible → UV → X-ray → Gamma

84. Frequency and Wavelength in EM Spectrum
  • As frequency increases, wavelength decreases.
  • Radio waves have long wavelengths.
  • Gamma rays have very short wavelengths.
  • All electromagnetic waves travel at speed c in vacuum.
  • Their energies differ because photon energy depends on frequency.
85. Radio Waves
  • Radio waves have relatively long wavelengths.
  • They are used in communication and broadcasting.
  • They are non-ionising electromagnetic radiation.
86. Microwaves
  • Microwaves are used in radar.
  • They are used in satellite communication.
  • Microwave ovens use microwaves to heat food through interaction primarily with polar molecules and ionic conduction.
  • Microwaves are non-ionising.
87. Infrared Radiation
  • Infrared lies beyond red in the electromagnetic spectrum.
  • Warm bodies emit significant infrared radiation.
  • Infrared is used in thermal imaging.
  • Remote controls commonly use infrared signals.
  • Infrared radiation is non-ionising.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Infrared → Heat/Thermal Imaging + Remote Controls

88. Ultraviolet Radiation
  • Ultraviolet lies beyond violet.
  • UV has higher frequency than visible light.
  • UV can cause sunburn and biological damage.
  • UV contributes to vitamin D synthesis in skin.
  • Ozone in the atmosphere absorbs much of the harmful solar UV.
  • UV is used in sterilisation and fluorescence applications.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

UV → Sunburn + Sterilisation

89. X-Rays
  • X-rays have higher frequency than ultraviolet radiation.
  • X-rays are ionising radiation.
  • They can penetrate soft tissue more readily than dense bone.
  • They are used in medical imaging.
  • Wilhelm Conrad Röntgen discovered X-rays in 1895.
  • Röntgen received the first Nobel Prize in Physics in 1901.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Röntgen → X-rays → 1895

90. Gamma Rays
  • Gamma rays are very high-frequency electromagnetic radiation.
  • They are ionising.
  • They can originate from nuclear transitions and other high-energy processes.
  • Gamma rays have high penetrating power.
  • They are used in radiotherapy and sterilisation under controlled conditions.
91. Human Eye — Optical Basics
  • The eye forms an image on the retina.
  • The eye lens is a converging lens system.
  • Cornea provides a major part of the eye's refractive power.
  • The eye lens fine-tunes focus.
  • Retina contains photoreceptor cells.
  • The image formed on the retina is real and inverted.
  • The brain interprets visual information.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Retina Image → Real + Inverted

92. Accommodation
  • Accommodation is the ability of the eye to change optical power to focus objects at different distances.
  • Ciliary muscles alter the shape of the eye lens.
  • For near objects, lens becomes more strongly curved and power increases.
  • For distant objects, lens becomes relatively thinner and power decreases.
93. Near Point of Normal Eye
  • Near point is the nearest distance at which the eye can focus comfortably.
  • For a normal young adult eye, the conventional textbook value is approximately 25 cm.
  • It is also called the least distance of distinct vision.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Least Distance of Distinct Vision → 25 cm

94. Far Point of Normal Eye
  • Far point is the farthest distance clearly visible without accommodation strain.
  • For a normal eye, far point is effectively at infinity.
95. Myopia
  • Myopia is short-sightedness.
  • Near objects are seen clearly.
  • Distant objects appear blurred.
  • Image of distant object tends to form in front of the retina.
  • Myopia is corrected using a concave lens.
  • Concave lens has negative power.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Myopia → Concave Lens

96. Hypermetropia
  • Hypermetropia is long-sightedness or farsightedness.
  • Distant objects are generally clearer than near objects.
  • Image of a near object tends to form behind the retina without adequate accommodation.
  • It is corrected using a convex lens.
  • Convex lens has positive power.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Hypermetropia → Convex Lens

97. Presbyopia
  • Presbyopia is age-related reduction in accommodation.
  • It results mainly from reduced flexibility of the lens and changes in accommodative mechanism.
  • Near point moves farther away.
  • Reading glasses with convex power may be required.
  • Bifocal or progressive lenses may be used when near and distance corrections are both needed.
98. Astigmatism
  • Astigmatism results from unequal curvature of cornea or lens in different meridians.
  • Different orientations may focus differently.
  • Cylindrical lenses are commonly used for correction.
  • Astigmatism can coexist with myopia or hypermetropia.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Astigmatism → Cylindrical Lens

99. Cataract
  • Cataract is clouding of the natural eye lens.
  • It reduces transparency and vision.
  • Cataract is commonly treated surgically by removing the cloudy lens and implanting an artificial intraocular lens.
  • Cataract is not corrected simply by ordinary spectacle lenses.
100. Persistence of Vision
  • Visual sensation persists briefly after light stimulation changes.
  • Traditional textbook descriptions often cite persistence of vision when explaining apparent continuous motion in rapid image sequences.
  • Modern perception of motion involves more complex visual processing than persistence alone.
  • Films and animations present rapidly changing frames to create apparent motion.
101. Simple Microscope
  • A simple microscope is essentially a convex lens of short focal length.
  • The object is placed within the focal length.
  • It forms a virtual, erect and magnified image.
  • A magnifying glass is a simple microscope.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Simple Microscope → Convex Lens

102. Compound Microscope
  • Compound microscope uses at least two lens systems.
  • Objective lens forms a magnified real intermediate image.
  • Eyepiece magnifies that intermediate image.
  • It is used to observe very small objects.
  • Short focal-length objective provides high magnification.
103. Astronomical Telescope
  • A telescope is used to observe distant objects.
  • Refracting telescopes use lenses.
  • Reflecting telescopes use mirrors.
  • Astronomical telescopes increase angular size and light-gathering ability.
  • Objective has large aperture to collect more light.
104. Refracting Telescope
  • Refracting telescope uses a convex objective lens.
  • Objective forms a real image.
  • Eyepiece magnifies the image.
  • Chromatic aberration can affect refracting telescopes.
105. Reflecting Telescope
  • Reflecting telescope uses a concave mirror as primary light collector.
  • Mirrors avoid chromatic aberration.
  • Large astronomical telescopes are commonly reflecting telescopes.
  • Isaac Newton built an early practical reflecting telescope.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Newtonian Telescope → Reflecting Telescope

106. Periscope
  • A simple periscope uses two plane mirrors or prisms.
  • Mirrors are often arranged at 45°.
  • It allows viewing over or around obstacles.
  • Submarines historically used periscopes for viewing above water.
107. Kaleidoscope
  • Kaleidoscope uses multiple reflection.
  • It typically uses mirrors inclined to each other.
  • Coloured objects form repeated symmetrical patterns.
  • The principle is repeated reflection.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Kaleidoscope → Multiple Reflection

108. Camera
  • A camera uses a converging lens system.
  • It forms a real inverted image on a sensor or film.
  • Aperture controls amount of light.
  • Shutter controls exposure time.
  • Focusing changes optical arrangement to make image sharp.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Camera Image → Real + Inverted

109. Photographic Aperture
  • Aperture is the opening through which light enters a camera.
  • Larger aperture allows more light.
  • Smaller f-number corresponds to a larger aperture in photographic notation.
  • Aperture also affects depth of field.
110. Pinhole Camera
  • A pinhole camera has no lens.
  • It works using rectilinear propagation of light.
  • It forms a real inverted image.
  • Smaller pinhole improves sharpness up to a point but reduces brightness.
  • Extremely small pinholes produce diffraction blur.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Pinhole Camera → Straight-Line Propagation

111. Mirage
  • A mirage is an optical phenomenon caused by refraction through layers of air having different temperatures and refractive indices.
  • Total internal reflection or strong bending can contribute in certain mirage conditions.
  • On hot roads, the apparent image of the sky can resemble water.
  • A mirage is not actual water.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Mirage → Atmospheric Refraction

112. Twinkling of Stars
  • Stars appear to twinkle because of atmospheric refraction through turbulent layers of air.
  • Starlight passes through regions of changing refractive index.
  • Apparent brightness and position fluctuate rapidly.
  • Stars behave nearly as point sources, so the effect is noticeable.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Twinkling of Stars → Atmospheric Refraction

113. Why Planets Usually Twinkle Less
  • Planets appear as small extended disks rather than point sources.
  • Fluctuations from different parts average out.
  • Therefore, planets generally twinkle much less than stars.
114. Advance Sunrise and Delayed Sunset
  • Atmospheric refraction makes the Sun visible when it is geometrically slightly below the horizon.
  • Sunrise is observed slightly earlier than it would be without atmosphere.
  • Sunset is observed slightly later.
  • The effect is due to refraction through Earth's atmosphere.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Early Sunrise + Late Sunset → Atmospheric Refraction

115. Redshift
  • Redshift is shift of observed spectral features toward longer wavelengths.
  • Receding astronomical objects can show Doppler/cosmological redshift.
  • Redshift is important in studying expansion of the universe.
116. Blueshift
  • Blueshift is shift toward shorter wavelengths.
  • Approaching sources can produce blueshift.
  • Blueshift corresponds to increased observed frequency in a Doppler interpretation.
📌 Remember

Receding → Redshift

Approaching → Blueshift

117. Photoelectric Effect
  • Photoelectric effect is emission of electrons from a material when suitable electromagnetic radiation strikes it.
  • Albert Einstein explained the photoelectric effect using light quanta.
  • Photon energy is hf.
  • A threshold frequency is required for a given material.
  • Increasing light intensity below threshold frequency does not cause photoemission.
  • Einstein received the 1921 Nobel Prize in Physics primarily for his explanation of the photoelectric effect.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Einstein → Photoelectric Effect → Photon Concept

118. Wave-Particle Duality
  • Light behaves as a wave in interference and diffraction.
  • Light behaves as particles in phenomena such as the photoelectric effect.
  • Photons possess energy and momentum.
  • Wave-particle duality is a basic principle of quantum physics.
119. Important Scientists and Light
  • Isaac Newton → Dispersion and corpuscular ideas.
  • Christiaan Huygens → Wave theory and Huygens' principle.
  • Thomas Young → Interference and double-slit experiment.
  • Augustin-Jean Fresnel → Wave optics and diffraction.
  • James Clerk Maxwell → Light as electromagnetic wave.
  • Max Planck → Quantum hypothesis.
  • Albert Einstein → Photoelectric effect.
  • Wilhelm Röntgen → X-rays.
  • Willebrord Snell → Refraction law.
120. Important Light Formulae
  • Speed in medium → v = c/n.
  • Photon energy → E = hf = hc/λ.
  • Law of reflection → i = r.
  • Mirror relation → f = R/2.
  • Mirror formula → 1/f = 1/v + 1/u.
  • Mirror magnification → m = −v/u.
  • Snell's Law → n₁ sin i = n₂ sin r.
  • Refractive index → n = c/v.
  • Apparent depth relation → n ≈ Real depth/Apparent depth.
  • Critical angle → sin C = 1/n for medium-to-air case.
  • Lens formula → 1/f = 1/v − 1/u.
  • Lens magnification → m = v/u.
  • Lens power → P = 1/f.
  • Lenses in contact → P = P₁ + P₂ + ...
  • Photon energy → E ∝ f and E ∝ 1/λ.
121. Important Units
  • Wavelength → metre.
  • Frequency → hertz.
  • Speed of light → m/s.
  • Focal length → metre.
  • Lens power → dioptre.
  • Refractive index → No unit.
  • Angle → degree or radian depending on context.
  • Photon energy → joule or electronvolt.
122. Must-Memorise Mirror Facts
  • Plane mirror → Virtual, erect, same size.
  • Concave mirror → Converging.
  • Convex mirror → Diverging.
  • Convex mirror → Always virtual, erect, diminished.
  • Shaving mirror → Concave.
  • Rear-view mirror → Convex.
  • Plane mirror → Lateral inversion.
  • Spherical mirror → R = 2f.
123. Must-Memorise Lens Facts
  • Convex lens → Converging.
  • Concave lens → Diverging.
  • Concave lens → Always virtual, erect, diminished for real object.
  • Magnifying glass → Convex lens.
  • Myopia → Concave lens.
  • Hypermetropia → Convex lens.
  • Astigmatism → Cylindrical lens.
  • Convex power → Positive.
  • Concave power → Negative.
  • Power unit → Dioptre.
124. Must-Memorise Optical Phenomena
  • Blue sky → Rayleigh scattering.
  • Red sunset → Scattering.
  • Rainbow → Refraction + dispersion + internal reflection.
  • Twinkling stars → Atmospheric refraction.
  • Early sunrise → Atmospheric refraction.
  • Mirage → Atmospheric refraction.
  • Optical fibre → Total internal reflection.
  • Diamond sparkle → Total internal reflection.
  • Prism colours → Dispersion.
  • Tyndall effect → Colloidal scattering.
  • Young experiment → Interference.
  • Polarisation → Transverse nature of light.
125. TNPSC Traps
  • Light does not require a material medium.
  • Speed of light is greatest in vacuum.
  • Frequency remains unchanged when light crosses a stationary boundary.
  • Wavelength changes when light enters a different medium.
  • Angles of incidence and reflection are measured from the normal.
  • Diffuse reflection still obeys reflection laws.
  • Plane mirror forms a virtual image.
  • Convex mirror always forms virtual, erect and diminished image.
  • Rear-view mirrors are convex.
  • Shaving mirrors are concave.
  • Refraction occurs because light speed changes.
  • Rarer to denser → bends toward normal.
  • Denser to rarer → bends away from normal.
  • Refractive index has no unit.
  • Optical density and mass density are different.
  • Total internal reflection requires denser-to-rarer travel.
  • TIR also requires incidence above critical angle.
  • Optical fibre works on TIR.
  • Convex lens is converging.
  • Concave lens is diverging.
  • Concave lens power is negative.
  • Convex lens power is positive.
  • Dioptre is unit of lens power.
  • Violet is deviated more than red by a glass prism.
  • Red has longest wavelength in visible spectrum.
  • Violet has highest visible frequency.
  • Rainbow is not caused by reflection alone.
  • Blue sky is caused mainly by scattering.
  • Twinkling of stars is caused mainly by atmospheric refraction.
  • Planets twinkle much less because they are extended sources.
  • Myopia → Concave lens.
  • Hypermetropia → Convex lens.
  • Astigmatism → Cylindrical lens.
  • Retina image is real and inverted.
  • Camera image is real and inverted.
  • Pinhole camera works without a lens.
  • Polarisation proves transverse nature.
  • Interference and diffraction prove wave behaviour.
  • Photoelectric effect supports particle behaviour.
126. Ultra-Short Memory Chain
  • Light → EM wave.
  • c → 3 × 10⁸ m/s.
  • Photon → hf.
  • Reflection → i = r.
  • Plane mirror → Virtual, erect.
  • Concave → Converging.
  • Convex mirror → Wide field.
  • R = 2f.
  • Refraction → Speed change.
  • Snell → n₁sin i = n₂sin r.
  • n → c/v.
  • TIR → Denser to rarer.
  • Fibre → TIR.
  • Convex lens → Converging.
  • Concave lens → Diverging.
  • Lens power → 1/f.
  • Unit → Dioptre.
  • Prism → Dispersion.
  • VIBGYOR → Colours.
  • Violet → Most deviation.
  • Red → Least deviation.
  • Blue sky → Scattering.
  • Sunset red → Scattering.
  • Rainbow → Dispersion + reflection/refraction.
  • Myopia → Concave.
  • Hypermetropia → Convex.
  • Astigmatism → Cylindrical.
  • Young → Interference.
  • Maxwell → EM light.
  • Einstein → Photoelectric.
  • Röntgen → X-rays.
Rapid Revision — TNPSC Most Expected
  • Nature of light? → Electromagnetic radiation.
  • Does light require a material medium? → No.
  • Speed of light in vacuum? → Approximately 3 × 10⁸ m/s.
  • Photon-energy formula? → E = hf.
  • Visible-light range approximately? → 400–700 nm.
  • Longest visible wavelength? → Red.
  • Shortest visible wavelength? → Violet.
  • Highest visible frequency? → Violet.
  • Light travelling in straight lines demonstrates? → Rectilinear propagation.
  • Complete shadow? → Umbra.
  • Partial shadow? → Penumbra.
  • Law of reflection? → Angle of incidence equals angle of reflection.
  • Angles measured from? → Normal.
  • Image formed by plane mirror? → Virtual, erect and same size.
  • Plane-mirror image distance? → Equal to object distance.
  • Left-right reversal in mirror? → Lateral inversion.
  • Converging mirror? → Concave mirror.
  • Diverging mirror? → Convex mirror.
  • Rear-view mirror? → Convex mirror.
  • Why convex mirror is used in vehicles? → Wide field of view.
  • Shaving mirror? → Concave mirror.
  • Dentist mirror? → Concave mirror.
  • Relation between radius and focal length of spherical mirror? → R = 2f.
  • Convex mirror image? → Always virtual, erect and diminished.
  • Concave mirror with object inside focus? → Virtual, erect and enlarged.
  • Mirror formula? → 1/f = 1/v + 1/u.
  • Mirror magnification? → −v/u.
  • Refraction means? → Bending due to change in light speed between media.
  • Law governing refraction? → Snell's Law.
  • Snell's Law? → n₁ sin i = n₂ sin r.
  • Absolute refractive index? → n = c/v.
  • Does refractive index have a unit? → No.
  • Rarer to denser medium bends? → Toward normal.
  • Denser to rarer bends? → Away from normal.
  • Does frequency change during refraction? → No.
  • Does wavelength change? → Yes.
  • Object under water appears? → Shallower / raised.
  • Emergent ray through rectangular glass slab? → Parallel to incident ray with lateral displacement.
  • Two conditions for total internal reflection? → Denser to rarer medium and incidence angle greater than critical angle.
  • Optical fibre works on? → Total internal reflection.
  • Diamond sparkle mainly due to? → Total internal reflection and dispersion.
  • Convex lens is? → Converging lens.
  • Concave lens is? → Diverging lens.
  • Image by concave lens for a real object? → Virtual, erect and diminished.
  • Convex lens with object inside focus gives? → Virtual, erect and magnified image.
  • Lens formula? → 1/f = 1/v − 1/u.
  • Lens power formula? → P = 1/f in metres.
  • SI unit of lens power? → Dioptre.
  • Convex-lens power sign? → Positive.
  • Concave-lens power sign? → Negative.
  • Power of lenses in contact? → Sum of individual powers.
  • White light splitting into colours? → Dispersion.
  • Colour sequence? → VIBGYOR.
  • Colour deviated most by glass prism? → Violet.
  • Colour deviated least? → Red.
  • Scientist who demonstrated white light spectrum using prism? → Isaac Newton.
  • Primary rainbow red colour located? → Outer edge.
  • Primary rainbow violet located? → Inner edge.
  • Primary rainbow mainly involves how many internal reflections? → One.
  • Secondary rainbow involves? → Two internal reflections.
  • Why is sky blue? → Rayleigh scattering of shorter wavelengths.
  • Why are sunrise and sunset red? → Shorter wavelengths are scattered away over long atmospheric path.
  • Rayleigh scattering dependence? → Approximately 1/λ⁴.
  • Why are danger signals red? → Long wavelength and relatively less scattering.
  • Tyndall effect occurs due to? → Scattering by colloidal particles.
  • Wave phenomenon demonstrated by Young's double slit? → Interference.
  • Constructive interference gives? → Bright fringe.
  • Destructive interference gives? → Dark fringe.
  • Bending of light around small openings? → Diffraction.
  • Property proving transverse nature of light? → Polarisation.
  • Electromagnetic-spectrum order? → Radio, microwave, infrared, visible, ultraviolet, X-ray, gamma.
  • Which travels fastest in vacuum: radio or gamma? → Both travel at c.
  • Infrared commonly used in? → Thermal imaging and remote controls.
  • Ultraviolet used in? → Sterilisation.
  • X-rays discovered by? → Wilhelm Röntgen.
  • X-ray discovery year? → 1895.
  • Image formed on retina? → Real and inverted.
  • Least distance of distinct vision for normal young eye? → About 25 cm.
  • Far point of normal eye? → Infinity.
  • Short-sightedness? → Myopia.
  • Myopia corrected with? → Concave lens.
  • Long-sightedness? → Hypermetropia.
  • Hypermetropia corrected with? → Convex lens.
  • Age-related loss of accommodation? → Presbyopia.
  • Astigmatism corrected with? → Cylindrical lens.
  • Clouding of eye lens? → Cataract.
  • Simple microscope uses? → Convex lens.
  • Camera forms what type of image? → Real and inverted.
  • Pinhole camera works on? → Rectilinear propagation of light.
  • Periscope uses? → Reflection by mirrors/prisms.
  • Kaleidoscope works on? → Multiple reflection.
  • Twinkling of stars caused by? → Atmospheric refraction.
  • Why do planets twinkle less? → Their extended images average atmospheric fluctuations.
  • Early sunrise and delayed sunset caused by? → Atmospheric refraction.
  • Mirage caused mainly by? → Refraction through air layers of different refractive index.
  • Photoelectric effect explained by? → Albert Einstein.
  • Einstein's photoelectric explanation supports? → Particle nature of light.
  • Wave nature of light shown by? → Interference and diffraction.
  • Scientist who showed light is electromagnetic? → James Clerk Maxwell.
  • Scientist associated with wave theory of light? → Christiaan Huygens.
  • Scientist associated with double-slit interference? → Thomas Young.
  • Core TNPSC memory line? → Reflection → i = r; Refraction → Snell; TIR → Optical fibre; Convex → Converging; Concave → Diverging; Myopia → Concave; Hypermetropia → Convex; Blue sky → Scattering.

Mie Scattering: Inelastic scattering caused by pollen, dust, smoke and other particles in the lower atmosphere

Raman scattering: When sun light passes through a gas or liquid the entire light is scattered by the atmosphere
